claim: To date there are no therapies for patients with congenital myopathies.
source: To date there are no therapies for patients with congenital myopathies, muscle disorders causing poor quality of life of affected individuals.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of treatment options for congenital myopathies, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In approximately 30% of the cases, patients with congenital myopathies carry either dominant or recessive mutations in the ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) gene.
source: In approximately 30% of the cases, patients with congenital myopathies carry either dominant or recessive mutations in the ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) gene
evidence: This is a statistical claim about the prevalence of RYR1 mutations in congenital myopathy patients, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Recessive RYR1 mutations are accompanied by reduction of RyR1 expression and content in skeletal muscles.
source: recessive RYR1 mutations are accompanied by reduction of RyR1 expression and content in skeletal muscles and are associated with fiber hypotrophy and muscle weakness.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research findings in the field.

claim: Recessive RYR1 mutations are associated with fiber hypotrophy and muscle weakness.
source: recessive RYR1 mutations are accompanied by reduction of RyR1 expression and content in skeletal muscles and are associated with fiber hypotrophy and muscle weakness.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field about the phenotypic consequences of recessive RYR1 mutations.

claim: Muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit increased content of class II histone deacetylases.
source: Importantly, muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit increased content of class II histone deacetylases and of DNA genomic methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research findings referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit increased DNA genomic methylation.
source: Importantly, muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit increased content of class II histone deacetylases and of DNA genomic methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research findings referenced in the manuscript.

claim: A mouse model was created carrying the p.Q1970fsX16+ p.A4329D RyR1 mutations, which are isogenic to those carried by a severely affected child suffering from a recessive form of RyR1-related multi-mini core disease.
source: We recently created a mouse model knocked-in for the p.Q1970fsX16+ p.A4329D RyR1 mutations, which are isogenic to those carried by a severely affected child suffering from a recessive form of RyR1-related multi-mini core disease.
evidence: This claim describes the creation of a mouse model, which is a methodological statement supported by the authors' prior work.

claim: The phenotype of the RyR1 mutant mice recapitulates many aspects of the clinical picture of patients carrying recessive RYR1 mutations.
source: The phenotype of the RyR1 mutant mice recapitulates many aspects of the clinical picture of patients carrying recessive RYR1 mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' prior characterization of the mouse model.

claim: Treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle strength.
source: Here, we show that treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle strength, RyR1 protein content, and muscle ultrastructure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including grip strength measurements and running wheel tests.

claim: Treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves RyR1 protein content.
source: Here, we show that treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle strength, RyR1 protein content, and muscle ultrastructure.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased RyR1 protein levels in treated mice.

claim: Treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle ultrastructure.
source: Here, we show that treatment of the mutant mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle strength, RyR1 protein content, and muscle ultrastructure.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing improved CRU structure and mitochondrial content.

claim: This study provides proof of concept for the pharmacological treatment of patients with congenital myopathies linked to recessive RYR1 mutations.
source: This study provides proof of concept for the pharmacological treatment of patients with congenital myopathies linked to recessive RYR1 mutations.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by a massive release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) via the opening of the ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1).
source: Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by a massive release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) via the opening of the ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1), a calcium release channel, which is localized in the SR terminal cisternae (Rios and Pizarro, 1991; Endo, 1977; Fleischer and Inui, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research in the field of muscle physiology.

claim: RyR1 is a calcium release channel localized in the SR terminal cisternae.
source: Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by a massive release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) via the opening of the ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1), a calcium release channel, which is localized in the SR terminal cisternae (Rios and Pizarro, 1991; Endo, 1977; Fleischer and Inui, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research in the field.

claim: The signal causing the opening of the RyR1 is the depolarization of the sarcolemmal membrane, which is sensed by voltage-dependent L-type Ca2+ channels (dihydropyridine receptor [DHPR]) located in invaginations of the sarcolemma referred to as transverse tubules (TTs).
source: The signal causing the opening of the RyR1 is the depolarization of the sarcolemmal membrane, which is sensed by voltage-dependent L-type Ca2+ channels (dihydropyridine receptor [DHPR]) located in invaginations of the sarcolemma referred to as transverse tubules (TTs) (Rios and Pizarro, 1991; Franzini-Armstrong and Jorgensen, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research in muscle physiology.

claim: Communication between DHPR and RyR1 occurs in specialized intracellular junctions between TT and SR called Ca2+ release units (CRUs).
source: Communication between DHPR and RyR1 occurs in specialized intracellular junctions between TT and SR called Ca2+ release units (CRUs).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in muscle physiology.

claim: Skeletal muscle relaxation is brought about by SR Ca2+ uptake via the activity of the sarco(endo)plasmic reticulum CaATPAses (SERCA).
source: Skeletal muscle relaxation is brought about by SR Ca2+ uptake via the activity of the sarco(endo)plasmic reticulum CaATPAses (SERCA) (MacLennan, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established research.

claim: Dis-regulation of Ca2+ signals due to defects in key proteins (RyR1 and DHPR) involved in excitation-contraction (EC) coupling (ECC) is the underlying feature of several neuromuscular disorders.
source: Dis-regulation of Ca2+ signals due to defects in key proteins (RyR1 and DHPR) involved in excitation-contraction (EC) coupling (ECC) is the underlying feature of several neuromuscular disorders (Jungbluth et al., 2018; Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in RYR1 are causative of malignant hyperthermia (MH; MIM #145600).
source: In particular, mutations in RYR1, the gene-encoding RyR1, are causative of malignant hyperthermia (MH; MIM #145600), central core disease (CCD; MIM #11700), specific forms of multi-minicore disease (MmD; MIM # 255320), and centronuclear myopathy (Jungbluth et al., 2018; Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020; MacLennan and Philips, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research.

claim: Mutations in RYR1 are causative of central core disease (CCD; MIM #11700).
source: In particular, mutations in RYR1, the gene-encoding RyR1, are causative of malignant hyperthermia (MH; MIM #145600), central core disease (CCD; MIM #11700), specific forms of multi-minicore disease (MmD; MIM # 255320), and centronuclear myopathy (Jungbluth et al., 2018; Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020; MacLennan and Philips, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research.

claim: Mutations in RYR1 are causative of specific forms of multi-minicore disease (MmD; MIM # 255320).
source: In particular, mutations in RYR1, the gene-encoding RyR1, are causative of malignant hyperthermia (MH; MIM #145600), central core disease (CCD; MIM #11700), specific forms of multi-minicore disease (MmD; MIM # 255320), and centronuclear myopathy (Jungbluth et al., 2018; Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020; MacLennan and Philips, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research.

claim: Mutations in RYR1 are causative of centronuclear myopathy.
source: In particular, mutations in RYR1, the gene-encoding RyR1, are causative of malignant hyperthermia (MH; MIM #145600), central core disease (CCD; MIM #11700), specific forms of multi-minicore disease (MmD; MIM # 255320), and centronuclear myopathy (Jungbluth et al., 2018; Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020; MacLennan and Philips, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research.

claim: RYR1 mutations result mainly in four types of channel defects.
source: A great deal of data has shown that RYR1 mutations result mainly in four types of channel defects (Treves et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: One class of mutations (dominant, MH-associated) causes the channels to become hypersensitive to activation by electrical and pharmacological stimuli.
source: One class of mutations (dominant, MH-associated) causes the channels to become hypersensitive to activation by electrical and pharmacological stimuli (MacLennan and Philips, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The second class of RYR1 mutations (dominant, CCD-associated) results in leaky channels leading to depletion of Ca2+ from SR stores.
source: The second class of RYR1 mutations (dominant, CCD-associated) results in leaky channels leading to depletion of Ca2+ from SR stores (Treves et al., 2008; Lawal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A third class of RYR1 mutations also linked to CCD causes EC uncoupling, whereby activation of the voltage sensor Cav1.1 is unable to cause release of Ca2+ from the SR.
source: A third class of RYR1 mutations also linked to CCD causes EC uncoupling, whereby activation of the voltage sensor Cav1.1 is unable to cause release of Ca2+ from the SR (Avila et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The fourth class comprises recessive mutations, which are accompanied by a decreased content of mutant RyR1 channels on SR membranes.
source: The fourth class comprises recessive mutations, which are accompanied by a decreased content of mutant RyR1 channels on SR membranes (Wilmshurst et al., 2010; Monnier et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients with congenital myopathies such as MmD carrying recessive RYR1 mutations belonging to class 4 channel defects, typically exhibit non-progressive proximal muscle weakness.
source: Patients with congenital myopathies such as MmD carrying recessive RYR1 mutations belonging to class 4 channel defects, typically exhibit non-progressive proximal muscle weakness (Jungbluth et al., 2005; Klein et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The reduced muscle strength in patients with recessive RYR1 mutations is consistent with the lower RyR1 content observed in adult muscle fibers that should result in a decrease of Ca2+ release from the SR.
source: This reduced muscle strength is consistent with the lower RyR1 content observed in adult muscle fibers that should result in a decrease of Ca2+ release from the SR (Wilmshurst et al., 2010; Monnier et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013; Jungbluth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The decrease of RyR1 expression is associated with moderate fiber atrophy, which may additionally contribute to the decrease of muscle strength.
source: The decrease of RyR1 expression is also associated with moderate fiber atrophy, which may additionally contribute to the decrease of muscle strength.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about the contribution of fiber atrophy to muscle weakness.

claim: Muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit striking epigenetic changes, including altered expression of microRNAs.
source: In addition to the depletion of RyR1 protein, muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit striking epigenetic changes, including altered expression of microRNAs, an increased content of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5, and hypermethylation of more than 3600 CpG genomic sites (Zhou et al., 2006; Rokach et al., 2015; Bachmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit an increased content of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5.
source: In addition to the depletion of RyR1 protein, muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit striking epigenetic changes, including altered expression of microRNAs, an increased content of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5, and hypermethylation of more than 3600 CpG genomic sites (Zhou et al., 2006; Rokach et al., 2015; Bachmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit hypermethylation of more than 3600 CpG genomic sites.
source: In addition to the depletion of RyR1 protein, muscles of patients with recessive RYR1 mutations exhibit striking epigenetic changes, including altered expression of microRNAs, an increased content of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5, and hypermethylation of more than 3600 CpG genomic sites (Zhou et al., 2006; Rokach et al., 2015; Bachmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In muscle biopsies from four patients, hypermethylation of one of the internal RYR1 CpG islands correlated with the increased levels of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5.
source: Importantly, in muscle biopsies from four patients, hypermethylation of one of the internal RYR1 CpG islands correlated with the increased levels of HDAC-4 and HDAC-5 (Rokach et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The dHT mouse model carries the p.Q1970fsX16 + p.A4329D RyR1 mutations.
source: Such a mouse model carries the p.Q1970fsX16 + p.A4329D RyR1 mutations (Elbaz et al., 2019) and will henceforth be referred to as double heterozygous (dHT).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Characterization of the muscle phenotype of dHT mice demonstrated that it faithfully recapitulates not only the physiological and biochemical changes, but also the major muscle epigenetic signatures observed in muscle biopsies from MmD patients.
source: Characterization of the muscle phenotype of dHT mice demonstrated that it faithfully recapitulates not only the physiological and biochemical changes, but also the major muscle epigenetic signatures observed in muscle biopsies from MmD patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior characterization work by the authors.

claim: Treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength.
source: Our results show that treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength, increases RyR1 protein content, and improves muscle morphology, that is, the treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1) and mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes increases RyR1 protein content.
source: Our results show that treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength, increases RyR1 protein content, and improves muscle morphology, that is, the treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1) and mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes improves muscle morphology.
source: Our results show that treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength, increases RyR1 protein content, and improves muscle morphology, that is, the treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1) and mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1).
source: Our results show that treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength, increases RyR1 protein content, and improves muscle morphology, that is, the treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1) and mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing improved CRU structure.

claim: The treatment partially rescues mitochondria.
source: Our results show that treatment of dHT mice with drugs targeting epigenetic enzymes rescues muscle strength, increases RyR1 protein content, and improves muscle morphology, that is, the treatment partially rescues CRUs (the intracellular sites containing RyR1) and mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing improved mitochondrial content and morphology.

claim: The peak blood concentration of TMP269 was achieved approximately 1 hr after injection.
source: The peak blood concentration of TMP269 was achieved approximately 1 hr after injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: The circulating levels of TMP269 decay within 12 hr.
source: The circulating levels of TMP269 decay within 12 hr (Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: The class II HDAC inhibitor diffuses into skeletal muscle.
source: Importantly, the class II HDAC inhibitor diffuses into skeletal muscle (Appendix 1—figure 1B), and as expected, its concentration profile in skeletal muscle follows that observed in blood.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1B.

claim: The concentration profile of TMP269 in skeletal muscle follows that observed in blood.
source: Importantly, the class II HDAC inhibitor diffuses into skeletal muscle (Appendix 1—figure 1B), and as expected, its concentration profile in skeletal muscle follows that observed in blood.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data and represents an expected outcome.

claim: The concentration of TMP269 in muscle is adequate to induce an inhibitory effect on class IIa HDACs activity.
source: Although the level of TMP269 accumulating in skeletal muscle is lower compared to that present in blood, its concentration in muscle is adequate to induce an inhibitory effect on class IIa HDACs activity (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and inference from the pharmacokinetic data.

claim: Administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks resulted in hypomethylation of 165 protein-coding genes in soleus muscles.
source: Administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks resulted in hypomethylation of 165 protein-coding genes (Supplementary file 1) in soleus muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide DNA methylation analysis data.

claim: Most of the hypomethylated genes belong to pathways involved in gene transcription, kinase activity, and membrane targeting.
source: Gene Ontology analysis showed that most of the hypomethylated genes belong to pathways involved in gene transcription, kinase activity, and membrane targeting (Appendix 2—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of the methylation data.

claim: Administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks increases the acetylation of Lys residues in total homogenates from FDB fibers isolated from WT and dHT mice.
source: Importantly, administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks increases the acetylation of Lys residues (Appendix 2—figure 2A and Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 1; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 3; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 4; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 5) and of H3K9 (Appendix 2—figure 2B and D and Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 1; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 3; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 4; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 5) in total homogenates from flexor digitorum brevis (FDB) fibers isolated from wild type (WT) and dHT mice, compared to that observed in fibers from vehicle-treated WT and dHT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Appendix 2—figure 2.

claim: Administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks increases the acetylation of H3K9 in total homogenates from FDB fibers isolated from WT and dHT mice.
source: Importantly, administration of TMP269 + 5-Aza for 15 weeks increases the acetylation of Lys residues (Appendix 2—figure 2A and Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 1; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 3; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 4; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 5) and of H3K9 (Appendix 2—figure 2B and D and Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 1; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 2; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 3; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 4; Appendix 2—figure 2—source data 5) in total homogenates from flexor digitorum brevis (FDB) fibers isolated from wild type (WT) and dHT mice, compared to that observed in fibers from vehicle-treated WT and dHT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Appendix 2—figure 2.

claim: The inhibition of the deacetylation activity of class IIa HDACs by TMP269 occurs in the nuclei.
source: This result unequivocally indicates that the inhibition of the deacetylation activity of class IIa HDACs by TMP269 occurs in the nuclei.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of increased H3K9 acetylation, a nuclear histone modification.

claim: In the absence of TMP269 + 5-Aza treatment, the level of H3K9 acetylation in myonuclei from FDB fibers isolated from dHT mice is 50% lower compared to WT.
source: In addition, Appendix 2—figure 2 also shows that in the absence of TMP269 + 5-Aza treatment, the level of H3K9 acetylation in myonuclei from FDB fibers isolated from dHT mice is 50% lower compared to WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 2—figure 2.

claim: The drugs reach skeletal muscles where they exerted their biological function.
source: Furthermore, these results confirm that the drugs reach skeletal muscles where they exerted their biological function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed biochemical changes in muscle tissue.

claim: Administration of TMP269 alone does not induce any change in the grip strength of WT mice.
source: Administration of each drug singly, namely TMP269 or 5-Aza alone, does not induce any change in the grip strength of WT (Figure 1A, top left and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Administration of 5-Aza alone does not induce any change in the grip strength of WT mice.
source: Administration of each drug singly, namely TMP269 or 5-Aza alone, does not induce any change in the grip strength of WT (Figure 1A, top left and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The combined drug treatment did not affect the grip strength of WT mice.
source: The combined drug treatment did not affect the grip strength of WT mice (Figure 1A, top right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: In dHT mice, TMP269 alone causes a small but significant increase of grip strength after 10 weeks of treatment.
source: In dHT mice, TMP269 alone causes a small but significant increase of grip strength after 10 weeks of treatment (Figure 1A, low left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The increased grip strength in dHT mice was more evident by the combined drug treatment.
source: However, the increased grip strength in dHT mice (Figure 1A, lower right panel) was more evident by the combined drug treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The effect of combined drug treatment on grip strength became apparent 4/5 weeks after starting the drug treatment and peaked at 10 weeks.
source: In particular, this effect became apparent 4/5 weeks after starting the drug treatment and peaked at 10 weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The combined drug treatment rescues approximately 20% of muscle grip strength in dHT mice.
source: The combined drug treatment rescues approximately 20% of muscle grip strength in dHT mice (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for raw data on the grip strength of individual dHT mice before and after treatment with TMP269 + 5-Aza).
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: On day 20 the total running distance of WT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 70% greater compared to that of vehicle-treated dHT mice.
source: Nevertheless, on day 20 the total running distance of WT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 70% greater compared to that of vehicle-treated dHT mice: the total running distance of vehicle-treated WT and dHT mice was 186.27 ± 16.70 km n = 4 vs. 59.93 ± 21.38 km n = 5, respectively (mean ± SD, Mann-Whitney two-tailed test, calculated over the 20 days of running, *p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by running wheel data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment of dHT mice with TMP269 + 5-Aza has a remarkable effect on the total running distance.
source: On the other hand, treatment of dHT mice with TMP269 + 5-Aza has a remarkable effect on the total running distance (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by running wheel data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The beneficial effect of TMP269 + 5-Aza on running distance begins 1 week after treatment commencement.
source: The beneficial effect begins 1 week after treatment commencement, and on day 20 the total running distance achieved by dHT mice injected with TMP269 + 5-Aza was two times higher compared to that covered by dHT mice injected with vehicle alone (Figure 1B, lower panel; Mann-Whitney two-tailed test; on day 20, p = 0.041)
evidence: This claim is supported by running wheel data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: On day 20 the total running distance achieved by dHT mice injected with TMP269 + 5-Aza was two times higher compared to that covered by dHT mice injected with vehicle alone.
source: The beneficial effect begins 1 week after treatment commencement, and on day 20 the total running distance achieved by dHT mice injected with TMP269 + 5-Aza was two times higher compared to that covered by dHT mice injected with vehicle alone (Figure 1B, lower panel; Mann-Whitney two-tailed test; on day 20, p = 0.041): the total running distance for vehicle-treated and drug-treated dHT mice was 59.93 ± 21.38 km n = 5 and 125.90 ± 16.39 km n = 5, respectively (mean ± SD, Mann-Whitney two-tailed test, calculated over the 20 days of running *p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by running wheel data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The longer running distance was associated with an increased median cruise speed of the drug-treated dHT mice compared to vehicle-treated dHT mice.
source: The longer running distance was also associated with an increased median cruise speed of the drug-treated dHT mice compared to vehicle-treated dHT mice (Figure 1B, right panels) (Mann-Whitney two-tailed test, calculated over the 20 days running period, *p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by running wheel data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The epigenetic modifying drugs most likely affect a number of genes, which in turn leads to an improvement of the in vivo muscle performance of the dHT mice.
source: The epigenetic modifying drugs most likely affect a number of genes, which in turn leads to an improvement of the in vivo muscle performance of the dHT mice
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism of drug action.

claim: The improvement in muscle performance may result from an improvement of the mechanical properties of skeletal muscles and/or by an influence of the drugs on the metabolic pathways of muscles.
source: the latter effect may result from an improvement of the mechanical properties of skeletal muscles and/or by an influence of the drugs on the metabolic pathways of muscles.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: The averaged specific twitch peak force induced by a single action potential in EDL from dHT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 37% of that obtained from EDLs from WT mice.
source: The averaged specific twitch peak force induced by a single action potential in EDL from dHT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 37% of that obtained from EDLs from WT mice (64.92 ± 13.93 mN/mm2, n = 10 vs. 171.24 ± 29.32** mN/mm2, n = 8, respectively; mean ± SD; ANOVA followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test **p < 0.01; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The peak force developed after twitch stimulation of soleus muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 67% of that of obtained in soleus muscles from WT littermates injected with vehicle.
source: The peak force developed after twitch stimulation of soleus muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle alone was approximately 67% of that of obtained in soleus muscles from WT littermates injected with vehicle (67.55 ± 11.26 mN/mm2, n = 10 vs. 96.58 ± 25.78* mN/mm2, n = 8, respectively; mean ± SD; ANOVA followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test *p < 0.05; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The combined drug treatment does not affect the force developed by EDL muscles.
source: While the combined drug treatment does not affect the force developed by EDL muscles, we found that it induces a 25% increase of the twitch force in soleus muscles from dHT mice compared to that obtained from vehicle-treated dHT mice
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The combined drug treatment induces a 25% increase of the twitch force in soleus muscles from dHT mice compared to that obtained from vehicle-treated dHT mice.
source: we found that it induces a 25% increase of the twitch force in soleus muscles from dHT mice compared to that obtained from vehicle-treated dHT mice (84.61 ± 14.06 mN/mm2, n = 13 vs. 67.55 ± 11.26* mN/mm2, n = 10, respectively; mean ± SD; ANOVA followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test *p < 0.05; Figure 2G and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The maximal specific tetanic force developed in EDL muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle was approximately 20% lower compared to that of EDL muscles from WT mice.
source: The maximal specific tetanic force developed in EDL muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle was approximately 20% lower compared to that of EDL muscles from WT mice (373.76 ± 73.16* mN/mm2, n = 10 vs. 452.97 ± 89.59 mN/mm2, n = 8, respectively; mean ± SD; ANOVA followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test *p < 0.05; Figure 2B and D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: There was no effect of the combined drug treatment on the maximal specific force developed by EDL muscles isolated from dHT mice.
source: We found no effect of the combined drug treatment on the maximal specific force developed by EDL muscles isolated from dHT mice (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The maximal specific tetanic force generation observed in soleus muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle was 13% lower compared to WT.
source: The maximal specific tetanic force generation observed in soleus muscles from dHT mice injected with vehicle was 13% lower compared to WT (276.29 ± 40.04* mN/mm2, n = 10 vs. 315.86 ± 56.96 mN/mm2, n = 8, mean ± SD; ANOVA followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test *p < 0.05) (Figure 2F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2.

claim: The combined drug treatment fully rescues the maximal tetanic force of slow twitch muscles.
source: Contrary to what we observed in EDL muscles, the combined drug treatment fully rescues the maximal tetanic force of slow twitch muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo muscle force measurements presented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Treatment with TMP269 + 5-Aza causes no changes in the content of the fiber type composition of soleus muscles.
